title: LLM Inference Challenges — Building the Mental Model for Modern Inference Systems
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been exploring how modern LLM inference systems actually work internally.
What started with a simple question around KV cache slowly expanded into:

batching
GPU memory
multi-GPU inference
distributed serving
replicas
GPU communication
and finally runtime behavior during generation
While writing these articles, I noticed something interesting myself.
Many concepts keep reappearing:

KV cache
batching
parallelism
replicas
scheduling
GPU communication
At first I thought I was repeating things too much.
But over time I realized something: these concepts keep reappearing because modern inference systems themselves are deeply interconnected.
So before moving into:

vLLM internals
paged attention
continuous batching
advanced schedulers
I wanted to take one step back and review the foundation we have built so far.
Part 1 — Understanding KV Cache
We started with one of the most important concepts in inference systems: KV cache.
This article explored:

why transformers repeatedly recompute attention
how KV cache avoids redundant computation
why generation becomes faster after caching
and how memory usage grows during inference
This became the starting point for understanding why inference systems are fundamentally memory-sensitive systems.
Understanding KV Cache
Part 2 — Memory Challenges During Inference
After understanding KV cache, the next question became: what happens when memory usage keeps growing?
This article explored:

memory fragmentation
duplication
dynamic allocation problems
why serving systems struggle with memory efficiency
and why inference becomes difficult at scale
This was also where the connection between user concurrency and memory pressure started becoming visible.
Memory Challenges During Inference
Part 3 — GPU Utilization & Batching
This article focused on one core idea: GPUs are efficient only when we keep them busy.
We explored:

why single requests underutilize GPUs
how batching improves throughput
why requests are grouped together
and how serving systems try to maximize utilization
This became the foundation for understanding scheduling later.
GPU Utilization & Batching
Part 4 — Why We Need Multiple GPUs
At this stage, one question became unavoidable: why is one GPU not enough anymore?
This article explored:

model size vs GPU memory
what parameters and weights actually are
why large models cannot fit into one GPU
and why throughput requirements also force distributed systems
This was the transition point into multi-GPU inference.
Why We Need Multiple GPUs
Part 5 — Understanding Tensor Parallelism
Once we understood why one GPU is insufficient, the next step was understanding how models are split across GPUs.
This article explored:

what tensors actually are
how weights are represented as tensors
how tensor parallelism splits tensors across GPUs
and how multiple GPUs cooperate on the same layer computation
This introduced the idea that one layer itself may require many GPUs working together.
Understanding Tensor Parallelism
Part 6 — Understanding Pipeline Parallelism
After tensor parallelism, the next question became: what if even splitting tensors is not enough?
This article explored:

splitting transformer layers into stages
how activations move through pipeline stages
why pipeline bubbles happen
and how tensor + pipeline parallelism work together in real systems
This was where the inference system started feeling much more like distributed infrastructure.
Understanding Pipeline Parallelism
Part 7 — Understanding Data Parallelism
At this point, the infrastructure picture became much larger.
This article explored:

how entire model replicas are duplicated
why data parallelism scales concurrent users
how replicas maintain independent KV cache
and how tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism combine together
This article also connected all three forms of parallelism into one complete mental model.
Understanding Data Parallelism
Part 8 — Distributed Serving & Request Routing
Once replicas were clear, the next question became: how are requests actually managed?
This article explored:

load balancers
routers
request scheduling
session affinity
distributed serving systems
and what a “replica” physically means
This was the point where the mental model started shifting from: “running a model”
to:
“operating a distributed GPU system.”
Distributed Serving & Request Routing
Part 9 — GPU Communication & Networking
As systems scaled across many GPUs and servers, communication itself became a major topic.
This article explored:

NVLink
NVSwitch
InfiniBand
NCCL
inter-node communication
all-reduce operations
and why networking becomes critical in large inference systems
This was also where replicas started feeling less like servers and more like distributed supercomputing systems.
GPU Communication & Networking
Part 10 — Understanding Prefill vs Decode
This article became one of the most important runtime concepts so far.
We explored:

why prompt processing is highly parallel
why generation becomes sequential
why decode underutilizes GPUs
why pipeline bubbles appear
and why scheduler design becomes so important
This article connected almost everything learned earlier:

batching
KV cache
replicas
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
and distributed serving
into one runtime mental model.
Understanding Prefill vs Decode
What Comes Next?
At this point, the foundation feels much stronger.
We now understand:

how requests flow
how GPUs cooperate
how replicas scale
how communication happens
and why inference systems become difficult during decode
The next stage will focus much more on:

vLLM architecture
continuous batching
paged attention
scheduler design
and modern inference optimizations
And honestly, this is where inference systems start becoming even more interesting.
